newsitem.title: HONG KONG: IMF confident of HK's future fiscal autonomy.
newsitem.headline: IMF confident of HK's future fiscal autonomy.

text.p: International Monetary Fund (IMF) chief Michel Camdessus expressed confidence on Friday that Hong Kong would maintain its financial autonomy under Chinese rule.

Camdessus held up Hong Kong as a shining example of fiscal success and said the British colony's prudent monetary and exchange rate policy had "created an environment of macroeconomic stability and investor confidence".

The IMF's managing director expressed confidence the Sino-British treaties governing the handover, which enshrine the principle of "one country-two systems" permitting Hong Kong considerable autonomy and fiscal independence would prevail.
Hong Kong, a British colony for more than 150 years, reverts to China at midnight on June 30, 1997.

The arrangements for Hong Kong's quasi-central bank, the Hong Kong Monetary Authority (HKMA), and China's central bank, the People's Bank of China, to operate as two mutually independent but cooperative monetary authorities had been clearly established, Camdessus told an IMF-HKMA conference.
Camdessus said China had a stake in maintaining Hong Kong's success.

"History, geographic location, openness in trade and importance as a financial centre all point to its (Hong Kong's) critical interest in continued global integration -- an interest that is shared in China, in the region and in the rest of the world."
Hong Kong was "a prime example of an economy that has managed rapid structural transformation in an increasingly integrated world economy in a most successful way", he said.

Camdessus said the territory's sound legal and administrative framework, neutral civil service, impartial judicial system and freedom of information had all been critical to its economic success today "and will remain so".
Hong Kong was one of the world's most open economies and China was also moving towards greater openness, he said.
"One can easily see how promising this converging trend in China and Hong Kong is," he added.

Hong Kong could be assured of the IMF's "continuous interest" and IMF and World Bank members would have a chance to see one country-two systems in action at the bank's annual meeting in the territory in September, Camdessus said.
